60:40 Split Seat Design

A complete rear split-seat system engineered from structural frame through foam and upholstery, balancing crash-relevant structural requirements with day-to-day usability and a production-ready bill of materials.

Foam Pattern & Mould Development

The three-step tooling sequence used to take the cushion surface from a solid master pattern to a production-ready two-part mould.

1
Step 1 — Master Pattern

A solid master pattern of the cushion profile was built to the finished foam surface and edge geometry, including the rounded seat-front radius. This pattern became the single source of truth that every downstream mould and foam tool was measured against.

2
Step 2 — Mould Impression

A flexible impression was cast directly off the master pattern to capture every surface detail and radius with no loss of definition. This impression served as the working negative used to generate the hard tooling in the next step.

3
Step 3 — Two-Part Production Mould

The impression was used to produce a matched top-and-bottom mould set for foam moulding/casting, with locating features built in so the two halves close repeatably in the same position — ready to hand off for trial foam pours.

The Challenge

One seat, two independently folding halves, one shared envelope

A 60:40 split rear seat has to fold and latch independently on each side while sharing hardpoints, seatbelt anchorage, and trim surfaces with the fixed structure around it. The brief called for a design that felt like a single, continuous seat when up, but split cleanly and reliably when folded — without adding cost or assembly steps that would slow the line.

Approach

Structure-first, then foam and trim around it

I started from the load-bearing frame in UG NX, working out hinge and latch positions before layering in foam profiles and upholstery seams, so the visible surfaces never fought the mechanism underneath.

  • Modeled the split-seat frame, hinge brackets, and latch mechanism in UG NX, checking fold clearance against the surrounding trim in every position.
  • Coordinated foam density and profile with the supplier so the cushion held its shape without interfering with the fold line between the two seat sections.
  • Built the BOM and reviewed sheet-metal parts for laser-cutting and bending feasibility with the fabrication team before releasing for prototype.
  • Ran design reviews with upholstery and structural teams to catch interference issues on paper rather than on the prototype bench.
Reverse Engineering

3D laser scanning to validate frame geometry

The finished seat frame and folding mechanism were mounted and captured with a handheld 3D laser scanner to cross-check the physical build against the CAD surface and hardpoints. Scanning the actual welded assembly — hinges, latch, and mounting brackets included — surfaced small deviations between the released model and the fabricated part early, before they could show up as fitment or fold-clearance issues on the vehicle.

Design Validation

Cross-functional team (CFT) review

The design was walked through in a formal CFT review with design, structural, and manufacturing stakeholders in the room, referencing the physical buck alongside digital captures of the surface and mechanism. Feeding scan data and hardware straight into the review meant issues were flagged and assigned on the spot rather than surfacing after tooling had already been committed.

Vendor & Program Ownership

Vendor coordination, development, and costing

Beyond the CAD and release work, I owned the vendor-facing side of this program end to end — coordinating with the foam, mould, and fabrication vendors through pattern, mould, and trial-part development, and personally handling the costing so the design stayed within the program's target BOM cost as it moved toward tooling sign-off.

  • Coordinated with tooling and foam vendors through the master-pattern, mould-impression, and two-part production-mould stages shown above.
  • Tracked development timelines and trial-part quality with vendors, resolving fit and finish issues flagged in CFT review and scan comparison.
  • Owned part and tooling costing for the project — building part-wise cost breakdowns with vendors and tracking them against the target BOM cost through every development iteration, right up to tooling commitment.
Outcome

Fewer prototype cycles, one validated design

Catching fold and interference issues during CAD review — backed by laser-scan validation and a formal CFT sign-off — rather than after a physical build, meant fewer rounds of prototype-and-correct. The design was carried through to a feasibility-validated, costed state ready for tooling handoff.

Key Takeaway

"A split seat only looks simple from the outside — the discipline is making the mechanism disappear behind the surface, and making sure the vendor, the cost, and the CAD all agree before tooling is cut."
